subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Find the eccentricity, foci and directrices of the ellipse 4x² + y² − 8x + 2y + 1 = 0.

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Senior Inter Maths-2B (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.58 — SAQ chapter 8 Ellipse, answer 60, on a ★★★ SSP page (book p.49 chapter table). Printed appearance: AP 18 only — no TS tag is printed beside this question. Book p.58 prints NO margin '1 Mark' tags and no tick boxes for this question (unlike answers 58-59 on p.57), so the 1+1+1+1 mark split here is OURS, not the book's — patterned on the same '1 mark per result' shape the book prints for answers 58 and 59 in this same chapter, extended to credit the completing-the-square step because this question (unlike 58) starts from a genuinely unfactored general equation. Only three final results are asked (eccentricity, foci, directrices) — this question does NOT ask for the latus rectum, unlike Q58/Q59. This ellipse is VERTICAL (a < b): the book's own working correctly gets a = 1, b = 2 and states 'the ellipse is vertical', so the foci and directrix formulas use b·e and b/e, not a·e and a/e. Ellipse is an SAQ-ONLY unit on the book's IPE Blue Print (book p.5). No two-book union check and no board back-test were possible for Maths-2B (no second-year TSBIE BLM on hand; the book's five Guess Papers pp.118-127 are the orchestrator's back-test stand-in).

insider_note: The first thing to check after completing the square is whether a or b is bigger — this ellipse is vertical (b > a), so the foci sit on the y-axis, the opposite of the more common horizontal case.

steps.label: Standard form
steps.margin_note: First mark. Group the x-terms and y-terms, then complete each square.
steps.memory_tip: Divide by the number on the right at the end so the equation reads = 1.
steps.why: Completing the square in both x and y turns the general equation into the shifted standard form (x − h)²/a² + (y − k)²/b² = 1, so a² and b² can be read off directly.
common_mistakes: Adding 1 and 1 inside the brackets but forgetting the 4× multiplier when adding to the right-hand side.
Dividing the whole equation by 4 at the wrong stage and losing the separate a² and b².

steps.label: Eccentricity
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Here a² = 1, b² = 4, so a < b — the ellipse is vertical.
steps.memory_tip: When the y-denominator is bigger, use b² − a² over b² — the bigger axis is always on the bottom.
lines: Since a < b, the ellipse is vertical.
steps.why: For a vertical ellipse (b > a), the eccentricity formula swaps roles: it is the square root of b² − a², divided by b, because the major axis is now along y.
common_mistakes: Using the horizontal-ellipse formula √(a² − b²)/a by habit, without checking a < b first.
Getting a negative number under the root by subtracting in the wrong order.

steps.label: Foci
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Centre (h, k) = (1, −1); foci move along y = k ± be.
steps.memory_tip: Vertical ellipse: foci sit above and below the centre, on the y-axis direction.
steps.why: A vertical ellipse has its major axis along y, so the foci lie directly above and below the centre, at a distance be.
common_mistakes: Writing the foci as (1 ± be, −1), which puts them on the wrong axis.
Forgetting the shifted centre (1, −1) and writing (0, ±be).

steps.label: Directrices
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. y = k ± b/e, then rationalise by multiplying by √3.
steps.memory_tip: Vertical ellipse: directrices are horizontal lines, y = k ± b/e.
steps.why: The directrices of a vertical ellipse are horizontal lines y = k ± b/e — the reciprocal of the focus distance be, shifted by the same centre k.
common_mistakes: Writing the directrices as vertical lines (in terms of x) instead of horizontal lines (in terms of y).
Combining both directrices onto one line with a single ± sign in front of 4, which does not pair a sign correctly with each line.
